newsitem.title: USA: McVeigh deserves to die, U.S. bomb jury told.
newsitem.headline: McVeigh deserves to die, U.S. bomb jury told.

text.p: A prosecutor pleaded with jurors on Thursday to look into the eyes of convicted Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh and tell him he was a traitor who deserved to die.
But the defence urged the jury to spare the Gulf War veteran's life, saying that if he was put to death, he would take the secret of others who may be involved in the bombing to his grave.

"Look into the eyes of a coward and tell him you will have courage," prosecutor Beth Wilkinson said in a powerful final appeal to the jury that will decide whether McVeigh should be put to death or spend the rest of his life in prison for bombing the Alfred P. Murrah federal building, killing 168 people.
"Tell him he is no patriot. He is a traitor and he deserves to die," she said. "It's time, it's time for justice."
McVeigh stared without expression at the prosecutor during her 35-minute speech. His parents and sister, Jennifer, also in the courtroom, were grim-faced.
After being given instructions on the law by federal Judge Richard Matsch, the jury was expected later on Thursday to begin its deliberations on McVeigh's fate.

In her solemn statement to the hushed courtroom, Wilkinson stressed the enormity of McVeigh's crime, saying the April 19, 1995, attack was "the most bloody domestic terrorist act in the history of our country."

Wilkinson said McVeigh, a 29-year-old ex-soldier, killed more Americans on a single day than were killed in combat in the Gulf War. "There would not be enough seats in this courtroom if we could bring them all back today."

"We never knew such a dark and horrible place existed in America until Timothy McVeigh sent us there ... It is time for justice, it is time to impose the ultimate sanction on the man responsible for this terror ... Sentence Timothy McVeigh to death," she urged the jury.

Defence lawyers urged the jury to spare McVeigh's life, saying all Americans were partly to blame for the Oklahoma City bombing because the country failed to respond adequately to federal sieges at Ruby Ridge, Idaho, in 1992 and at Waco, Texas, in 1993 that became rallying cries for the right wing.
"Aren't we all implicated in some way in his crime?" chief defence attorney Stephen Jones said.

The defence has said McVeigh was deeply disturbed by the deaths of 80 Branch Davidian cult members in a confrontation with federal agents at Waco. Prosecutors said he bombed the Murrah building to avenge their deaths.
"Millions of Americans share Mr. McVeigh's views ... Mr. McVeigh acted on them," Jones said.

Jones said "the tragedy at Oklahoma City could have been avoided" if the government had been held accountable for the deaths of civilians at Waco and Ruby Ridge, where white separatist Randy Weaver's wife and son were killed in a shootout with federal agents.
Jones suggested that other unknown people were involved in the Oklahoma City bombing and if McVeigh was put to death the full story would never come out.
"Dead men do not tell tales. The government may not be the only people who want my client executed," Jones said, implying that others would be glad to see McVeigh take his secret to the grave.
Jones did not dispute McVeigh's guilt, saying: "He is not a demon, though surely his act was demonic."
But unlike other high-profile murders, the bombing was "a political crime. It is an ideological crime," Jones said.
McVeigh was found guilty on June 2 of 11 murder, conspiracy and bombing charges, all of which carry a possible death penalty.

During the penalty phase of the trial that began last week, the prosecution called dozens of survivors, bomb victims and rescue workers -- many in tears -- to testify about the horror of the bombing and the physical and emotional scars it left.

The defence called relatives, friends and former neighbours of McVeigh who said he was a cheerful child, a good student and a model soldier. The most poignant moment came on Wednesday when his mother and father took the stand to plead for his life.

Wilkinson said McVeigh's beliefs about Waco were "a misguided fantasy, not a reality" and the jury should dismiss McVeigh's attempt to blame the government for his crime. Several of the babies killed in the Murrah building were not even born when Waco happened, she said.
"This is the freest country in the world but what we must not tolerate as a free society is someone trying to impose their political will on the community through violence and terror."
